BED BUG DISCLOSURE AND INSPECTION — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for 123 Main St, Apt 4, Springfield · Acme Properties, LLC

PURPOSE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet describes California's bed bug disclosure and inspection statute, Civil Code §§ 1954.600-1954.605, as it may apply to the tenancy of the dwelling unit at 123 Main St, Apt 4, Springfield, as between Acme Properties, LLC and Jordan Lee. It states what California law provides on this subject. It does not itself serve as the written bed bug information notice the statute describes, and it does not determine whether a suspected or confirmed infestation exists at any specific property.

THE LEGISLATURE'S STATED FINDINGS ON BED BUG CONTROL
In enacting this chapter, the Legislature found and declared that controlling bed bugs is uniquely challenging because bed bug resistance to existing insecticidal control measures is significant, and that cooperation among landlords, tenants, and pest control operators is required for successful control; with such cooperation, most bed bug infestations can be successfully controlled. The Legislature further found that effective control is more likely when landlords and tenants are informed of best practices for bed bug control, that early detection and reporting is an important component of prevention, that tenants should not face retaliation for reporting a problem, and that lack of cooperation by landlords and tenants can undermine a pest control operator's efforts to identify and control an infestation.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Controlling bed bugs is uniquely challenging, as bed bug resistance to existing insecticidal control measures is significant. Cooperation among landlords, tenants, and pest control operators is required for successful control. With cooperation among landlords, tenants, and pest control operators, most bed bug infestations can be successfully controlled."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1954.600(a), California Civil Code, legislative finding on the difficulty of bed bug control and the need for cooperation (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1954.600.)
  "Early detection and reporting of bed bugs is an important component required for preventing bed bug infestations. Tenants should not face retaliation for reporting a problem."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1954.600(c), California Civil Code, legislative finding on early reporting and retaliation (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1954.600.)
  "Lack of cooperation by landlords and tenants can undermine pest control operator efforts to identify the presence of bed bugs and control an infestation."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1954.600(d), California Civil Code, legislative finding on the effect of lack of cooperation (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1954.600.)
  Known gap: This is a legislative findings-and-declarations section, not itself a set of operative legal duties -- the statement that "tenants should not face retaliation for reporting a problem" appears only here, as a finding, and this chapter does not itself set out a retaliation cause of action, remedy, or enforcement mechanism; whether other, separate California statutes prohibiting landlord retaliation apply to a bed bug report is outside this chapter's text and outside this document. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how one jurisdiction has framed bed bug control policy -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific tenancy. No California appellate decision construing this chapter was located in a CourtListener search conducted for this document; this document is accordingly based on statutory text alone.

WRITTEN BED BUG INFORMATION NOTICE REQUIRED BEFORE A NEW TENANCY
On and after July 1, 2017, before creating a new tenancy for a dwelling unit, a landlord must provide a written notice to the prospective tenant, in at least 10-point type, that includes -- but is not limited to -- general information about bed bug identification, behavior, and biology, the importance of cooperation for prevention and treatment, and the importance of prompt written reporting of suspected infestations to the landlord, with that information to be in substantially the statutorily specified form, plus the procedure for reporting a suspected infestation to the landlord. As a one-time transition matter, this same written notice also had to be provided to all other (already-existing) tenants by January 1, 2018.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "On and after July 1, 2017, prior to creating a new tenancy for a dwelling unit, a landlord shall provide a written notice to the prospective tenant as provided in this section. This notice shall be provided to all other tenants by January 1, 2018. The notice shall be in at least 10-point type and shall include, but is not limited to, the following:"
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1954.603, California Civil Code, timing, form, and minimum content of the required written bed bug notice (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1954.603.)
  "General information about bed bug identification, behavior and biology, the importance of cooperation for prevention and treatment, and the importance of and for prompt written reporting of suspected infestations to the landlord. The information shall be in substantially the following form:"
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1954.603(a), California Civil Code, required general bed bug information and reporting emphasis (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1954.603.)
  "The procedure to report suspected infestations to the landlord."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1954.603(b), California Civil Code, required reporting-procedure content (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1954.603.)
  Known gap: The January 1, 2018 deadline for delivering this notice to existing tenants was a one-time historical transition requirement tied to the chapter's July 1, 2017 operative date; it does not by its own terms recur at each lease renewal, and this document takes no position on whether a landlord in fact provided this notice by that date for any specific tenancy. The statute's "include, but is not limited to" language means the specified content is a floor, not a ceiling, on what the written notice may need to contain; this document does not attempt to reproduce the full statutorily specified informational text. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how one jurisdiction structures a pre-tenancy bed bug notice requirement -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific tenancy. No California case law construing this section was located.

LIMIT ON SHOWING, RENTING, OR LEASING A KNOWN-INFESTED VACANT UNIT
A landlord may not show, rent, or lease a vacant dwelling unit to a prospective tenant if the landlord knows that unit has a current bed bug infestation. This section does not itself impose a duty on a landlord to inspect a dwelling unit or the common areas for bed bugs where the landlord has no notice of a suspected or actual infestation -- but where an infestation is evident on visual inspection, the landlord is considered to have notice for purposes of this section.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "A landlord shall not show, rent, or lease to a prospective tenant any vacant dwelling unit that the landlord knows has a current bed bug infestation."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1954.602(a), California Civil Code, prohibition on showing, renting, or leasing a known-infested vacant unit (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1954.602.)
  "This section does not impose a duty on a landlord to inspect a dwelling unit or the common areas of the premises for bed bugs if the landlord has no notice of a suspected or actual bed bug infestation. If a bed bug infestation is evident on visual inspection, the landlord shall be considered to have notice pursuant to this section."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1954.602(b), California Civil Code, no freestanding inspection duty absent notice, and visual evidence as notice (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1954.602.)
  Known gap: This provision, by its own text, is limited to a vacant dwelling unit being shown, rented, or leased to a prospective tenant -- it does not on its face create a freestanding, ongoing duty to disclose an infestation in an occupied unit, in a different (e.g., adjacent) unit, or once a tenancy is already underway; whether some other disclosure duty applies to those situations is outside this chapter's text and outside this document. The statute's "knows" standard is defined here only in terms of what is evident on visual inspection; it does not address what other facts might or might not give a landlord notice. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how one jurisdiction limits leasing of a known-infested vacant unit -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific tenancy. No California case law construing "current bed bug infestation" or "notice" under this section was located.

ENTRY TO INSPECT FOR BED BUGS, AND THE TENANT'S COOPERATION DUTY
Entry to inspect a tenant's dwelling unit for bed bugs must comply with Civil Code § 1954, the general statute governing a landlord's right of entry. Entry to inspect any unit selected by the pest control operator, and to conduct followup inspections of surrounding units until bed bugs are eliminated, is itself treated as a "necessary" purpose for entry under Section 1954. For purposes of this chapter, a "pest control operator" means an individual holding a Branch 2 operator, field representative, or applicator license from the Structural Pest Control Board. Tenants must cooperate with the inspection to facilitate detection and treatment of bed bugs, including by providing information the pest control operator requests that is necessary to facilitate that detection and treatment.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Entry to inspect a tenant’s dwelling unit shall comply with Section 1954. Entry to inspect any unit selected by the pest control operator and to conduct followup inspections of surrounding units until bed bugs are eliminated is a necessary service for the purpose of Section 1954."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1954.604, California Civil Code, entry to inspect for bed bugs treated as a necessary purpose under the general entry statute (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1954.604.)
  "Tenants shall cooperate with the inspection to facilitate the detection and treatment of bed bugs, including providing requested information that is necessary to facilitate the detection and treatment of bed bugs to the pest control operator."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1954.604, California Civil Code, tenant's duty to cooperate with a bed bug inspection (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1954.604.)
  "For purposes of this chapter, the term “pest control operator” means an individual holding a Branch 2 operator, field representative, or applicator license from the Structural Pest Control Board."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1954.601, California Civil Code, definition of "pest control operator" for this chapter (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1954.601.)
  Known gap: Section 1954's own separate requirements for entry (such as its notice provisions) are incorporated by reference here, not restated in full in this chapter or in this document. The chapter states that followup inspection of "surrounding units" is a necessary service under Section 1954 but does not itself define how far "surrounding" extends. The tenant cooperation duty is stated in this chapter without this chapter itself specifying a remedy for a tenant's non-cooperation. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how one jurisdiction ties bed bug inspection to its general entry statute -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific tenancy. No California case law construing this section was located.

LANDLORD'S DUTY TO NOTIFY TENANTS OF THE PEST CONTROL OPERATOR'S FINDINGS
The landlord must notify the tenants of the units the pest control operator inspected of that operator's findings. This notification must be in writing and made within two business days of the landlord's receipt of the pest control operator's findings. Where the confirmed infestation is in a common area, all tenants -- not only those whose units were inspected -- must be provided notice of the findings.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "The landlord shall notify the tenants of those units inspected by the pest control operator pursuant to Section 1954.604 of the pest control operator’s findings. The notification shall be in writing and made within two business days of receipt of the pest control operator’s findings."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1954.605, California Civil Code, written notification of inspection findings within two business days (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1954.605.)
  "For confirmed infestations in common areas, all tenants shall be provided notice of the pest control operator’s findings."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1954.605, California Civil Code, all tenants notified for a confirmed common-area infestation (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1954.605.)
  Known gap: By its own terms, this notification duty runs to "the tenants of those units inspected" (plus, separately, to all tenants for a confirmed common-area infestation) -- it does not extend this specific duty to tenants of units that were not inspected outside that common-area situation. The two-business-day period is measured from the landlord's receipt of the pest control operator's findings, not from the date of the inspection itself, and this document does not address what counts as "receipt." This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how one jurisdiction structures a post-inspection notification duty -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific tenancy. No California case law construing this section was located.

ACKNOWLEDGMENT
This information sheet regarding bed bug disclosure and inspection requirements under California Civil Code §§ 1954.600-1954.605, concerning the dwelling unit at 123 Main St, Apt 4, Springfield as between Acme Properties, LLC and Jordan Lee, states California law as of the date below. It does not constitute legal advice about, and does not resolve, any specific infestation, inspection, or disclosure question.

Prepared: _______________________ Date: September 1, 2026

Oakland, California
